summary: For ages 5-7 (KS1 Y2 / Grades K-2), children learn that minibeasts live in specific micro-habitats suited to their needs: woodlice, worms and slugs in damp dark places (under logs, stones, leaf litter, in soil), pond skaters and dragonfly nymphs in water, aphids, caterpillars and ladybirds on sunny leaves, and butterflies among flowers. The core idea is the MATCH between creature and place, with a reason ('damp and dark so a woodlouse won't dry out'), learned through predict-then-check hunting and by reasoning about the consequence of a mismatch. Children should also practise careful handling — lifting gently and returning logs and stones exactly as found, and never placing a creature where it could come to harm.
misconceptions: 'Animals can live anywhere' — children don't yet see that a creature needs a place that suits it; a woodlouse can't thrive on a sunny wall.
'Habitat means the whole garden/wood' — the micro-habitat idea (the specific under-log, the specific pond edge) is the new precision at KS1.
'Dark, damp places are just where dirty bugs hide' — reframing: damp/dark IS the resource these creatures need.
'If I move it somewhere nicer it'll be happier' — moving a creature out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it.
Confusing a habitat (where it lives) with what it eats — related but distinct ideas.

activities.title: Bug detective: predict then check a micro-habitat
steps: Before looking, choose a micro-habitat (under a log, under a stone, in leaf litter, in the soil, at the pond edge, among flowers) and say out loud or tap picture-guesses for what you think lives there.
Lift the log/stone gently or look closely at the pond or flowerbed to check, and compare what you found against your guess.
For each creature found, say why it is there using a 'what it needs' idea (damp / dark / water / flowers / leaves).
Put every log and stone back exactly the way you found it before moving on.
activities.insight: Different micro-habitats hold different creatures because each creature needs the conditions that place provides — 'suited to its habitat' means the place gives the creature what it needs, not just 'that's where it happens to be'. Damp and dark are not where 'dirty bugs hide'; they are the resource these creatures need.

activities.title: Take me home: the consequence of a mismatch
steps: Using a screen simulation, a drawing, or spoken reasoning — never a real creature — think about a given creature in two places: a damp shaded spot versus a dry sunny patch.

Predict what would happen in each: a worm or woodlouse left on hot dry pavement would dry out and struggle, while under a damp log it settles. Never actually place a real creature in the sun to test this.
Explain in your own words why the creature needs its damp dark place to survive.
activities.insight: A creature is not free to live anywhere: moving it out of its suited micro-habitat can harm it, which is why 'suited to' matters — the need is about survival, not preference or choice.

activities.title: Compare two places side by side
steps: Look at two contrasting micro-habitats at once — a damp shaded under-log spot and a dry sunny wall or leaf.
Predict whether you'd find the SAME minibeasts in both, or different ones, and say why before checking.
List who you'd expect in each: damp-loving woodlice, worms, slugs under the log; sun-liking aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds on the sunny leaf.
Match each creature to the conditions it does best in (damp, dark, sunny, leafy).
activities.insight: Because different creatures need different conditions, the place helps predict which creatures you are likely to find — where you look changes what you find.

activities.title: Garden cross-section: where everyone lives
steps: Study a garden cross-section from pond to soil to leaf litter to canopy.
For each zone, name a creature that lives there and say one reason why ('why here?').
Add or draw a 'what it needs' card (damp / dark / water / flowers) linking each creature to its place.
activities.insight: A single garden contains many layered micro-habitats, each with residents suited to it — habitat means the specific place, not the whole garden.

activities.title: Sort and match creatures to habitats (check)
steps: Sort a set of minibeast cards into micro-habitats: pond / soil / under-log / sunny leaf; some creatures (like worms or slugs) can fit more than one damp place, so say why you chose.
Match each creature to its habitat.
Answer 'why do woodlice hide under logs?' choosing or saying the reason (damp and dark, so they don't dry out).
activities.insight: Children can reliably link each minibeast to the conditions its habitat provides.

activities.title: Ask the minibeast (optional light intro)
steps: Pose a question to a minibeast character — 'Where do you live and why?' — and listen to or read its reply ('I live under logs because it's damp and I'd dry out in the sun').
Follow up by predicting where a different creature would say it lives.
activities.insight: Each creature's home is tied to a need it can explain, offering a friendly way into the 'suited to' idea.

checkQuestion: You lift up a damp log in the shade, and you also look on a sunny leaf. Would you expect to find the SAME minibeasts in both places, or different ones? Why?
checkAnswer: Different ones. Minibeasts that like damp, dark places — woodlice, worms, slugs — live under the log, while ones that like sun and leaves — aphids, caterpillars, ladybirds — are on the leaf. Different creatures prefer different conditions, so where you look changes what you find.
